Lesson Overview: Author Presentation Planning

Lesson Focus

Lesson 6: Author Presentation Planning

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.COM.01 — Author presentation of creative work.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.COM.03 — Communication of craft reasoning; MLA.CW.WR.08 — Reflection on creative process and product.

What You Will Learn

  • Design a coherent presentation for a specific audience and time limit.
  • Select a representative excerpt through defensible criteria.
  • Integrate reading, craft analysis, revision evidence, and reflection.
  • Plan delivery and visual support without distracting from the creative work.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 6 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
presentation arcThe purposeful sequence that guides an audience through a presentation.The speaker moves from context to excerpt to reflection.
representative excerptA selected passage that accurately demonstrates important features of a larger work.The excerpt displays the story’s voice, conflict, and pacing.
signpostingBrief language that shows where a presentation is going or how ideas connect.“First, notice the repeated image” directs attention.
annotationA note marking evidence, delivery, timing, or interpretation.The script marks where to pause before the final line.
cadenceThe rhythmic rise, fall, stress, and timing of spoken language.Varied cadence prevents the reading from sounding mechanical.
vocal emphasisPurposeful stress placed on a word or phrase during speech.Emphasizing “still” reveals the character’s persistence.
rehearsal protocolA planned method for practicing, timing, observing, and revising delivery.The writer records one run, reviews it, and retests changes.
visual supportA chart, slide, image, or text display that clarifies spoken reasoning.One annotated image supports the explanation without replacing it.
audience calibrationAdjustment of context, language, and pacing to what listeners need.The speaker defines a specialized term for unfamiliar listeners.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which opening shows effective signposting?

A. “Here is my story.”

This announces the work but does not guide listeners toward a purpose or feature.

B. “Before I read, notice how the repeated train image changes from escape to obligation.”

Correct. It tells listeners what to attend to and prepares the later craft explanation.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 6 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: Engineer the Presentation Before Rehearsing

Step 1 — Define Audience, Purpose, and Constraint

Complete one sentence: “For an audience of ___, I will use ___ minutes to present ___ so listeners can understand/question/notice ___.” Time is a design constraint, not merely a stopwatch problem.

Step 2 — Select the Excerpt

CriterionTest
RepresentativeDoes it reveal a central craft pattern?
Self-containedCan listeners follow with 1–2 context sentences?
DiscussableDoes it support precise craft reasoning?
SpeakableCan it be delivered clearly within the allotted time?

Step 3 — Build the Five-Part Arc

  1. Frame: title, genre, central question, minimum context.
  2. Read: deliver the excerpt with intentional pace and emphasis.
  3. Analyze: name two exact craft choices and their effects.
  4. Revise: compare one meaningful before-and-after decision.
  5. Invite: offer an unresolved question or listening lens.

Pause and Choose: Select a Discussable Excerpt

A five-minute presentation analyzes how dialogue reveals a character’s divided loyalty. Which excerpt is the best choice?

A. The story’s longest descriptive paragraph because it contains the most words.
Weaker choice. Length does not establish relevance. If the passage does not display the central craft pattern, it cannot support precise analysis.
B. A brief exchange that listeners can follow with one context sentence and that contains the contrasting word choices the author will analyze.
Stronger choice. The excerpt is representative, self-contained, discussable, and speakable within the constraint.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 4 — Budget Time

For a five-minute presentation, a useful starting allocation is 0:30 Frame | 1:30 Read | 1:45 Analyze | 0:50 Revise | 0:25 Invite. Adjust by purpose, then time every section separately.

Step 5 — Design Visual Support

  • Display only text or images the audience must examine.
  • Use large readable type and high contrast.
  • Highlight evidence with labels, not color alone.
  • Keep one idea per visual.
  • Provide alternative text or spoken description for meaningful images.

Pause and Choose: Rehearse Diagnostically

A practice recording runs forty seconds over time, and the craft explanation is vague. What should the presenter revise first?

A. Cut unnecessary summary and replace general claims with two concise evidence-based explanations before polishing gestures.
Stronger choice. The problem is content design. A targeted revision improves both timing and intellectual clarity.
B. Speak much faster and add more animated gestures without changing the script.
Weaker choice. Faster delivery reduces comprehension, and gestures cannot replace missing evidence. Rehearsal should reveal what content needs revision.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 6 — Rehearse Diagnostically

  1. Record a full timed run.
  2. Mark where pace changes, filler appears, or evidence becomes vague.
  3. Ask a listener to name the purpose and two craft choices.
  4. Revise content before polishing gestures.
  5. Repeat until time, clarity, and delivery are stable.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 6 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Presentation Plans

Example 1 — Fiction Excerpt Choice

Options: an exciting climax requiring extensive context, or a quieter 180-word scene where a character repeatedly mislabels boxes while avoiding a farewell.

  1. Purpose: explain indirect characterization.
  2. The quieter scene is more representative and discussable.
  3. Frame with one sentence about the departure.
  4. Analyze repeated mislabeling, withheld dialogue, and pacing.
  5. Revision evidence: an early draft directly stated that the character feared leaving.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which excerpt is better for a short presentation on indirect characterization?

A. Use the exciting climax even though it needs several minutes of plot explanation.
Weaker response. The climax may be strong writing, but extensive context would consume the presentation and obscure the stated craft focus.
B. Use the 180-word box-labeling scene because repeated mislabeling, withheld dialogue, and pacing reveal avoidance with little setup.
Stronger response. This selection is representative, manageable, and rich in precise evidence that the presenter can explain within the available time.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Poetry Delivery Map

Excerpt: a 16-line poem whose sentence crosses three stanzas before ending with “home.”

  1. Mark breaths that preserve syntax without erasing line breaks.
  2. Slow slightly at stanza boundaries; do not stop automatically.
  3. Emphasize repeated directional verbs, not every image.
  4. Display the poem in high contrast with the syntactic path labeled.
  5. Explain how delayed completion makes “home” both destination and release.

Example 3 — Time-Cut Decision

Problem: A six-minute draft must fit four minutes.

  1. Protect the 60-second excerpt and two evidence-based craft claims.
  2. Cut plot summary from 90 to 20 seconds.
  3. Combine publication context with the opening.
  4. Reduce three revision examples to the most consequential one.
  5. Keep the reader invitation because it gives the ending purpose.

Principle: Cut redundancy before cutting evidence.

Transfer Grid

Plan each segment with four columns: Time | Spoken purpose | Evidence/visual | Delivery note.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Choose a brief passage for presenting how setting shapes a decision. State two selection criteria and one framing sentence.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: I would choose a self-contained passage where a closing station forces a visible choice. It needs clear setting evidence and minimal plot setup; I would frame it by saying the character must decide before the final train leaves.

page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 6 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Author Presentation Planning

Purpose

Design an author presentation that balances context, evidence, delivery, and audience engagement.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Support decisions with precise evidence from your portfolio work.

Source for Your Work

Presentation challenge: In five minutes, introduce the portfolio’s central growth story, share two short excerpts from different genres, and leave the audience with one memorable insight.

1. Plan Before You Work

Portfolio DecisionEvidence and Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each precisely.
Strongest current evidenceName the piece, passage, or feature.
Most important improvementDescribe the needed change and intended effect.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger author decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Explain every portfolio piece in order and read as quickly as possible to fit more information.
B. Build one clear through-line, select contrasting evidence, provide only needed context, and rehearse intentional delivery choices.

3. Apply the Lesson

Write a five-minute presentation script with an opening hook, a central growth claim, two strategically selected excerpts, transitions, and a purposeful close. Add delivery annotations for pace, pause, emphasis, and audience connection.

4. Revise with Purpose

Time and rehearse the presentation aloud. Cut or revise material to fit the limit and explain two delivery changes made after rehearsal.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to specific portfolio evidence.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on the audience.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves quality, coherence, or readiness.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Author Presentation Planning

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: A Presentation Without a Throughline

A writer plans to read three complete pieces in ten minutes, explain every revision, show twelve slides, and answer questions. The excerpts are strong, but the plan has no central message and leaves no time for transitions or audience response.

A presentation throughline is the central idea connecting every section. Audience cueing prepares listeners to understand why a detail or excerpt matters.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Identify three problems that would reduce audience understanding or engagement.
  2. What throughline could organize the presentation, and which material should be cut or shortened to serve it?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which plan demonstrates stronger author presentation design?

A. Speak faster and keep all material so the audience receives the maximum amount of information.
B. Choose one throughline, select brief representative excerpts, build purposeful transitions, and protect time for reflection and questions.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Create a 6–8 minute portfolio presentation plan and full script.

  1. Opening: Use a hook and state the throughline connecting your work.
  2. Portfolio context: Briefly identify the audience, forms, and organizing purpose.
  3. Excerpts: Select two contrasting excerpts; introduce each with a listening purpose and annotate delivery.
  4. Craft reflection: Explain how one technique and one major revision developed across the portfolio.
  5. Closing: Synthesize your growth and next goal, then invite one focused question.

Include a timed outline, any essential visual, and an accessibility plan for the audience.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Rehearse with a timer and record the actual length. Cut or reshape one section to strengthen the throughline and revise two delivery cues.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
